---
title: The Reading Experience
description: How docs.dev lays out prose around figures with pretext.
---

This is an ordinary documentation page. The heading above, this paragraph, the
code block below — all standard Fumadocs, exactly what you would write in any
other docs tool. The difference shows up when you reach for `<Spread>`.

```mdx
<Spread orb side="right" width="42%">
  Prose that flows around the figure, with **bold**, `code`, and [links](/) intact.
</Spread>
```

## Flowing prose

Wrap any Markdown in `<Spread>` and the prose flows around a figure, like a
magazine column. Notice the formatting survives the layout:

<Spread orb side="right" width="42%">
Everything inside a Spread is plain Markdown, so **bold**, *italic*, and inline
`code` all keep working while the text flows around the figure to the right.
The engine measures every run of text with [pretext](https://github.com/chenglou/pretext)
using nothing but canvas arithmetic — no `getBoundingClientRect`, no reflow —
then positions real, selectable DOM text on both sides of the obstacle at once.
That last part is something CSS Shapes cannot do: it only ever wraps on a single
side. Here the column genuinely narrows as it passes the orb and widens again
below it, and the words you are reading remain ordinary text nodes that a
crawler can index and a screen reader can announce.
</Spread>

## Text on both sides at once

Drop the figure in the middle of the column and the prose splits around it —
each line measured and placed on the left *and* the right of the figure. This
is the layout CSS floats and CSS Shapes fundamentally cannot express, and it
falls back to a clean stacked layout on small screens:

<Spread orb side="inline" width="34%" top={10}>
With `side="inline"` the figure sits centered while the paragraph continues
around **both** of its edges, like a proper magazine spread. Resize the window
and watch every line re-measure and re-break in real time — the geometry is
recomputed against the live column width, so the arrangement you design is the
arrangement readers get on any screen. On phones the figure gracefully goes
full-width and the prose stacks below it, because a two-sided flow at narrow
widths would leave slivers of unreadable text.
</Spread>

## How it stays fast and accessible

The server renders the prose above as a normal paragraph first, so search
engines and assistive technology always get clean text in reading order. After
the page hydrates, the client measures and repositions that same text into the
flowed layout. Same words, just placed differently — progressive enhancement,
not a hidden copy.

## Code blocks

Fenced code blocks are syntax-highlighted (Shiki), with a title, a copy button,
and line highlighting — no setup required.

```ts title="lib/measure.ts" {3-4}
import { prepare, layout } from '@chenglou/pretext';

const prepared = prepare(text, '16px Inter');
const { lineCount, height } = layout(prepared, 640, 32);

console.log(lineCount, height);
```

## Code tabs

Group related snippets into tabs — great for showing the same thing in multiple
languages or frameworks.

<Tabs items={['TypeScript', 'JavaScript']}>

```ts tab="TypeScript"
export function greet(name: string): string {
  return `Hello, ${name}`;
}
```

```js tab="JavaScript"
export function greet(name) {
  return `Hello, ${name}`;
}
```

</Tabs>

## Package-manager tabs

A single `package-install` block becomes npm / pnpm / yarn / bun tabs, and the
manager you pick is remembered across the whole site.

```package-install
@chenglou/pretext
```

## Lists

Everything you expect from Markdown works out of the box:

- Bullet lists with **bold**, *italic*, and `inline code`
- Links like [pretext](https://github.com/chenglou/pretext) survive editing
- Every item is editable in place
